author: ribeye
dek: Miami hit 100 degrees for only the second time ever, Dallas hit 105, and a Lima family learned their air conditioner has a flair for dramatic timing.
disclaimer: Parody: the Miller family of Lima is fictional. The Southern heat wave is real, as reported by Fox Weather in August 2026.
headline: Lima Family's Air Conditioner Quits on the Hottest Tuesday in 84 Years

ohio_quotes.quote: The air conditioner picked the hottest Tuesday in 84 years to quit. I respect the commitment to drama, but I do not appreciate it.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Tom Miller, Lima

ohio_quotes.quote: I told the kids the heat index is 115 and they asked if that meant school was canceled. It is August. There is no school. They still asked.
ohio_quotes.speaker: Carla Miller, Lima

ohio_story: LIMA, Ohio — Tom and Carla Miller of Lima did everything right. They changed the filter, they had the unit serviced in June, and they even bought one of those little window fans shaped like a robot for their daughter's room. Then Tuesday arrived with a heat index of 115 degrees across the South, and the Miller family's air conditioner made a noise like a lawn mower giving up on life and died on the spot.

"I stood in the driveway in 98-degree heat, holding a flashlight, pretending I knew what I was looking at," Tom said, wiping his forehead with a Kewpee napkin. "I have sat through Ohio State-Michigan games in a downpour and a three-hour rain delay at a Mud Hens game, but I have never lost a staring contest with a condenser unit." By evening, the family had retreated to the basement with a box fan, a cooler of ice, and the dog, Biscuit, who claimed the coolest square foot of concrete in Allen County and refused to negotiate.

Carla, meanwhile, spent the afternoon on the phone with three different repair companies, all of whom were booked solid until next week. The kids, Ben, 14, and Sophie, 11, took it about as well as could be expected, which is to say Ben has now declared preseason football practice "a form of cruel and unusual punishment" and Sophie has started a spreadsheet ranking every air-conditioned building in Lima, with the library currently in first place. The Millers are now weighing a drive to the Allen County Fair just to stand in front of the livestock fans, a plan Tom describes as "honestly pretty good" and Carla describes as "we are not cooling off next to a prize hog."
real_summary: A brutal heat wave gripped the Southern United States in the week of August 17, 2026, with more than 72 million people under Heat Alerts and more than 18 million under Extreme Heat Warnings. Feels-like temperatures reached 115 degrees in some places, and a Level 4 out of 4 extreme HeatRisk — the highest category — lingered across the Lower Mississippi Valley and the Southeast coast through Friday.

Nearly 50 record-high temperatures fell across the South that week, adding to what was already the hottest summer on record for 36 cities from Texas through the Carolinas and Florida, according to the FOX Forecast Center. Miami reached 100 degrees on Tuesday, August 18 — the city's hottest day in 84 years and only the second time in recorded history that Miami has reached triple digits. Dallas hit 105 degrees on Monday and could remain at or above 105 through the following Tuesday, which would be the city's longest such stretch since 1980. Oklahoma City reached 109 degrees, the first time it had done so after August 11 since record-keeping began.

Relief was only relative: even as a push of cooler Canadian air began breaking up the heat dome over the Southeast, triple-digit heat indices lingered from the Southern Plains to the Southeast coast, and intense heat was expected to persist through the weekend across parts of Oklahoma, North Texas, and the Texas Gulf Coast. According to NOAA, heat-related illnesses kill more Americans annually than any other type of extreme weather.
source_note: Fox Weather reporting, Aug. 17-20, 2026: Southern heat wave; more than 72 million under Heat Alerts; Miami's 100-degree day on Aug. 18.
